WASHINGTON — South Carolina Gov.

Nikki Haley, drawing on her personal biography as the daughter of Indian immigrants, urged Americans to resist the "angriest voices" of the political season in her speech Tuesday night following President Obama's State of the Union address.

Haley, speaking to a national audience from the first floor of the governor's residence in Columbia, presented a stark contrast to the heated rhetoric of the presidential campaign — where some GOP candidates are calling for mass deportations and a rejection of all Muslims over fears of terrorism and crime.
While calling for a more respectful tone in the immigration debate, she did not soften her stance against accepting Syrian refugees or stopping illegal immigration.
"We cannot continue to allow immigrants to come here illegally.
And in this age of terrorism, we must not let in refugees whose intentions cannot be determined," Haley said.
Haley delivered the GOP response to Obama's final State of the Union address at the request of Republican House Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell.
Haley, who turns 44 next week,is the first female and first minority governor of South Carolina, which made her a compelling choice for a Republican Party eager to reach more voters of color.
She's also a potential contender to be a vice presidential running mate to the Republican nominee, and her speech included a heavy dose of criticism of the Obama record.
Like Obama, however, Haley devoted much of her address to giving an optimistic view of the future.
Haley also argued the case for electing a Republican in November to succeed Obama.
She and her staff wrote the speech without input from national GOP leadership, Haley said recently.
She called it an address, not a response, to the president.
“I certainly am not one to compete against the president or try to imply that I could be," she said last week.
During Obama’s presidency, Republicans have used the high-profile event to showcase up-and-coming conservatives, including Ryan in 2011.
One year later, GOP presidential nominee Mitt Romney chose Ryan as his running mate.

Haley's selection to give Tuesday's address has heightened speculation she could be asked to be on the GOP ticket this year, especially as the party struggles to attract minority voters.South Carolina hosts the first presidential primary in the South on Feb. 20, and her endorsement is highly sought after.
Her speech also drew lessons from recent tragic events in South Carolina.
Haley last year successfully called for removal of the Confederate flag from the state Capitol grounds in response to a mass shooting at a prominent black church in Charleston in June.

In April, a police shooting of an unarmed black man in North Charleston brought swift action by law enforcement to fire the officer and charge him with murder, which helped South Carolina avoid the violent protests that played out in other states after police shootings.
Haley is among those Republican governors, many from the South, who have opposed Obama on several major policy fronts.

Haley has asked the federal government not to relocate Syrian refugees in South Carolina; she has not expanded Medicaid health coverage for lower-income Americans as allowed under the Affordable Care Act;and she opposes closing the military prison at Guantanamo Bay in Cuba.
Yet even at the White House, the choice of Haley to give the GOP response drew favorable reviews.

White House Chief of Staff Denis McDonough said Tuesday, before Haley's speech, that while he disagreed with some of Haley's policy positions, he commended her response to the shootings in Charleston.
White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest gave Haley credit for "taking a risk" on a speech that has tripped up other Republicans, such as former Louisiana Gov.
Bobby Jindal, whose 2009 speech was widely criticized.
"You've got to to admire somebody to take on that kind of risk where others have not succeeded," Earnest said.
Haley blamed both political parties for an increasingly frustrated electorate.
Tuesday night was far from Haley's first time in the Washington spotlight.
She often addresses the national media on behalf of the Republican Governors Association when it meets in Washington, and in September she spoke at the National Press Club.
Her selection to deliver Tuesday's speech, however, increases scrutiny of her record.
South Carolina’s child welfare agency has been unable to manage its child abuse and neglect cases, and dozens of children have died as a result.
In 2012, Haley reimbursed the state about $10,000 for using the state plane improperly.
And there remain pockets of persistent poverty and high unemployment in the state, according to state Democratic officials.
They also have criticized her refusal to expand the state’s Medicaid program using federal funds, which would increase access to affordable health care for many South Carolina residents.
“This is not a record that should be heralded or modeled,” said Jaime Harrison, chairman of the South Carolina Democratic Party.
